title: Earliest Finish for Two Rides
statement:
A theme park has land rides and water rides. Land ride i opens at time landStart[i] and takes landDuration[i] minutes. Water ride j opens at waterStart[j] and takes waterDuration[j] minutes.

A visitor must take exactly one land ride and exactly one water ride, in either order. A ride can be started at its opening time or any time later, and the second ride can start only after the first one finishes (it may start at the very moment the first ends). Waiting is allowed.

Return the earliest time at which the visitor can finish both rides.

examples.why: Land ride 0 runs 2–6, then the water ride runs 6–9. Every other plan ends at 10 or later.
Water first (1–6), wait until 10, then land (10–12). Land first would end at 17.
The land ride that opens first is a trap: it lasts until 21. Water 4–5 then land ride 1 at 5–7 is best.

constraints: 1 ≤ n, m ≤ 100 (n land rides, m water rides)
hints: Try both orders separately: land then water, and water then land.
Fix the order land then water. The water ride only cares about one thing from the land ride: when it ended. Which land ride gives the best end time?

The best first ride is simply the one that finishes earliest (start + duration). Then for each second ride the finish is max(firstEnd, start) + duration; take the minimum, and do the same with the roles swapped.

explain.intuition:
Fix the order, say land first. Whatever land ride you take, the only thing that matters afterwards is the moment it ends. Ending earlier never hurts: the water ride starts at max(landEnd, waterStart), which can only get smaller or stay the same. So take the land ride with the smallest start + duration, then try every water ride after it.

Do the same with water first, and return the better of the two orders. Each order is one pass to find the best first ride plus one pass over the second rides, so the brute force over all pairs shrinks to O(n + m).
steps: For every water ride j, the finish is max(bestLandEnd, waterStart[j]) + waterDuration[j]. Keep the minimum.
Compute bestWaterEnd the same way and try every land ride after it.
Return the smaller of the two results.
pitfalls: Starting the second ride at firstEnd without checking its own opening time. You must take max(firstEnd, start).
Choosing the first ride by earliest opening time instead of earliest end, as the third example shows.
Trying only one order. The second example needs water first.

solutions.title: Try every pair in both orders
solutions.idea: For each land ride and each water ride, compute both orders' finish times and keep the minimum.

solutions.title: Earliest-ending first ride, then scan
solutions.idea: In a fixed order, the best first ride is the one that ends earliest. Try every second ride after it, for both orders.

followups: There are 50 000 rides of each kind. Which solution still works?
The visitor must take three rides of three different kinds. How many orders are there, and does the same greedy idea extend?
lcTitle: Earliest Finish Time for Land and Water Rides I
